replies.author: @machteldvdb1185
replies.text:
Everything you mention regarding the medical bills is inaccurate. 

For a 7-day hospital stay in Belgium, you pay between €250 and €400 for a two-person room when you don't have an additional hospitalization insurance. Most working people get the additional hospitalization insurance for themselves and their family through their employer at a very low rate.

Furthermore, there is the Maximum Invoice for medical expenses (MAF) for low income people. The ceiling for MAF is €270.60 in 2026.
Once your family has paid that amount in co-payments within a single calendar year, your health insurance fund will fully reimburse any further co-payments for the remainder of the year.

This means that you exceed the MAF ceiling when you are hospitalized for 7 consecutive days. All medical bills that follow within the calendar year will be fully reimbursed.

replies.text: Hello, Belgium here. If you don't live in the full countryside where you might have a bus/hour or less, you don't want to take a car to visit or to live in Belgium. You don't want to drive in cities because of traffic jams, high prices for entries, forbidden entries and high prices for car parks in and around the cities if available. You also get fined and you don't even know why. There are plenty of metros and trams and busses in every city, also in between cities,  and if you are late in the evening, you might rent a bicycle, take an uber. A lot of  traffic jams in between cities too, but if you want to visit the Ardennes, you might like to have a car. Rent one ore take a shared one, I do that for groceries. Flanders and Brussels are better off for busses than wallonia. Belgian people like to complain, but they don't compare with other countries. We use blablacar too in between cities or countries, it's a funny experience. So you have plenty of options at a decent price, cheaper than France or England for instance where you have the same troubles.
